title: From the Frankish Cradle to the Throne in the Tomb
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Herstal — the Pippinid hall on the Meuse (birthplace uncertain: Herstal? Aachen? Quierzy?)
stops.campa: A boy is born to Pepin the Short and Bertrada of the great foot, in one of the Pippinid halls along the Meuse — Herstal by the oldest habit of the family, though the cradle is nowhere fixed and the canon keeps its silence honestly. The Lorsch calendar will one day write the second of April against his name. He is Charles, grandson of the Hammer who broke the Saracens at Poitiers. The Meuse runs grey past the villa; the mayors of the palace already rule kings who do not rule.
suggested_refs: Kalendarium of Lorsch (birth-note of Charles)
the Pippinid villa lands of the Meuse valley
sources: Einhard, Vita Karoli 4 (birth and childhood passed over)

stops.name: Basilica of Saint-Denis — Pope Stephen anoints Pepin and his sons
stops.campa: Pope Stephen II, who has crossed the Alps in winter to beg the Frankish sword against the Lombards, rises in the abbey of the martyr Denis and pours the holy oil on Pepin, on Carloman, and on the boy Charles, twelve years old. In one act the papacy and the Franks are wed. The pope binds the Frankish nobles under pain of interdict never again to choose a king sprung from other loins. The boy feels the oil dry on his forehead; the throne of Peter has laid its hand on the house of Pepin forever.
stops.quote: …that they should never presume in time to come to choose a king sprung from the loins of any other line.
suggested_refs: Basilica of Saint-Denis
the holy ampulla and rite of Frankish anointing

stops.name: Saint-Denis — the death of Pepin the Short
stops.campa: Pepin, returning from crushing Aquitaine, is seized by fever at Saintes and carried north to die where he was anointed. On the twenty-fourth of September he gives back his soul at Saint-Denis and is buried, at his own bidding, face down before the threshold for the sins of his father. The realm is divided by Frankish custom between the two sons: Charles the elder takes the outer crescent of the kingdom, Carloman the rich inner lands. The brothers do not love each other. The abbey bells toll a king who made the crown real.
suggested_refs: tomb of Pepin the Short at Saint-Denis

stops.name: Noyon — Charles raised king of the Franks
stops.campa: On the ninth of October, in the cathedral city of Noyon, the magnates lift Charles on the shield of the Franks and set the crown on him, while on the same day at Soissons his brother Carloman is crowned over the other half. Two kings, one realm, one jealousy. Charles is twenty-six, tall, thick-necked, with the large clear eyes Einhard will remember; his voice is thinner than his frame. The oil of Saint-Denis, fourteen years dry, begins its work.
suggested_refs: Noyon Cathedral (later Gothic successor of the coronation church)

stops.name: Fronsac on the Dordogne — the first war fought alone
stops.campa: Aquitaine rises under old Hunald, and Carloman refuses his brother aid, turning home from Duasdives with his host. Charles goes on alone. He drives to the Dordogne and builds the fortress of Fronsac on its rock above the river, and from there sends envoys to Lupus, duke of the Gascons, demanding the rebel. Lupus, weighing the new king, hands Hunald over with his wife. The first war of the reign ends without a battle lost: the young king has learned that a fort, a demand, and patience can conquer a duchy.
suggested_refs: tertre de Fronsac above the Dordogne

stops.name: Samoussy — the death of Carloman
stops.campa: At the royal villa of Samoussy, on the fourth of December, King Carloman dies of a flux of blood at the nose and mouth, twenty years old. The rivalry that was ripening toward war — over Aquitaine, over the Lombard marriage their mother made and Charles repudiated — dissolves in a night. His widow Gerberga gathers her infant sons and flees, not to her brother-in-law but over the Alps to Desiderius the Lombard, and by that flight fixes the road Charles must one day take. He is buried at Reims. The whole realm hangs loose, waiting for one hand.
suggested_refs: royal villa of Samoussy
Carloman's tomb at Reims

stops.name: Corbeny — the whole realm his
stops.campa: Within days the great men of Carloman's kingdom — Wilchar the archbishop, Fulrad the chaplain, counts Warin and Adalhard — ride to Charles at the villa of Corbeny and commend themselves to him, passing over the dead king's sons in their cradles. There is no election, no war: the Franks simply turn, as a field turns to the sun. Charles receives their hands between his and is king of all the Franks. From this winter villa on the Laon road, the single reign begins that will not end for forty-three years.
suggested_refs: Corbeny (later shrine of Saint-Marcoul on the coronation road of French kings)

segments.name: The World-Pillar and the Iron Crown (772-774)

stops.name: Worms — the assembly decrees the Saxon war
stops.campa: At Worms on the Rhine the first great assembly of the sole reign gathers, and the king proposes war on the Saxons — the pagan neighbor that burns churches on the border and honors trees and springs. Thirty-three years of war are decreed in an afternoon, though no man there knows it. The host is blessed, the standards raised; the Franks march northeast into the woodland where the old gods still hold their courts. Einhard will write that no war was ever longer, crueler, or more full of toil.
suggested_refs: Worms on the Rhine, seat of Carolingian assemblies

stops.name: The Eresburg — the Saxon fortress stormed
stops.campa: The army comes up out of the Diemel valley against the Eresburg, the hill-fortress of the Saxons on its steep table of rock. The Franks take it by storm; the gates are burned, a garrison installed, and a church will stand where the rampart-shrine stood. From its height the king looks north into Saxony — forest to the edge of sight, no roads, no writing, no baptism. Somewhere in that green dark stands the pillar the Saxons say upholds the universe. He gives the order to march to it.
suggested_refs: Obermarsberg (Eresburg) plateau
church of Saints Peter and Paul, Obermarsberg

stops.name: The Irminsul — the world-pillar felled
stops.campa: In a sacred grove near the Eresburg stands the Irminsul, the universal column of the pagans, the trunk they say carries the sky. Charles comes to it with axes. For the Saxons this is the ending of the world; for the Franks it is the beginning of Saxony's salvation. The great pillar goes down, the grove is fired, and three days are spent destroying the sanctuary utterly. From under the shrine the Franks lift the treasure of generations — the gold and silver of a whole people's vows — and carry it away in the king's train. The sky, the chroniclers note, does not fall.
stops.quote: He destroyed this idol and carried away the gold and silver which he found there.
suggested_refs: the Externsteine rocks (later tradition's Irminsul site)
relief of the bent tree at the Externsteine

stops.name: The camp by the Irminsul — the spring at noon
stops.campa: A great drought lies on the land, and in the place where the Irminsul stood there is no water; the army, laboring at the destruction of the temple, begins to fail with thirst. Then at noon, while the host rests and no man is drawing or digging, water bursts from the ground in a stream — enough for the whole army, poured out by the grace of God in the very footprint of the felled idol. The Franks read the sign plainly: the God of the Christians waters His soldiers where the false pillar stood. The king lets the army drink, then finishes the burning.
stops.quote: Suddenly at noon, through the grace of God, while the army rested and nobody knew what was happening, so much water poured forth in a stream that the whole army had enough.
suggested_refs: the miracle-spring of the 772 campaign

stops.name: Geneva — the muster for Italy
stops.campa: Pope Hadrian's envoys have come by sea, since the Lombard holds the roads: Desiderius has seized the cities of Peter and demands the pope anoint Carloman's little sons kings of the Franks. Charles offers gold for peace three times; three times the Lombard refuses. So at Geneva, where the Rhone leaves the lake, the Frankish host divides in two: the king will take the Mont Cenis, his uncle Bernard the Great Saint Bernard, the two horns of an army closing on Lombardy. The lake lies flat and bright; beyond it the wall of the Alps, and beyond the wall, Italy.
suggested_refs: Lake Geneva and the Rhone gate to the passes

stops.name: The Cluses of Susa — the Lombard wall turned
stops.campa: Desiderius waits behind the ancient walls of the cluses, the fortified throat of the Susa valley, and the passes are barred. Then a Frankish detachment finds a path over the bare ridges — the canon remembers a nameless Lombard jongleur who sang the way, and later legend a mountain guide — and comes down behind the barrier. The Lombards wake to Franks above and Franks before them, abandon the works in a night without a battle, and stream back onto the plain. The gate of Italy stands open. Charles rides through the broken cluses under the October snow-light.
suggested_refs: the Chiusa di San Michele in the Val di Susa
Sacra di San Michele above the cluses

stops.name: Pavia — the siege of the Lombard capital begins
stops.campa: Desiderius shuts himself in Pavia, the brick-walled capital of the Lombards on the Ticino, and Charles, refusing the cost of a storm, sits down to starve it. He sends for Hildegard the queen and his children to winter with him before the walls: the siege will be a royal court in canvas. Adelchis the king's son has fled to Verona with Carloman's widow and her boys — the last loose threads of the Frankish succession, gathered conveniently under one distant roof. The rains come; the Franks build huts; Pavia begins its slow year of hunger.
suggested_refs: walls and towers of Pavia
San Michele Maggiore, coronation church of the Lombard kings

stops.name: Verona — the widow's sons taken
stops.campa: Leaving the siege lines, Charles marches on Verona, strongest of Lombard cities. It does not test him: Gerberga, Carloman's widow, comes out with her sons and gives herself into the hands of the brother-in-law she fled. Adelchis slips away east to end his days a Byzantine patrician, an exile with a title and no country. The canon then closes over the little princes — they pass from the record without a word, absorbed into the king's mercy or his silence. Charles returns to the siege with the last rival Carolingian blood riding in his baggage.
suggested_refs: Roman walls of Verona

stops.name: Rome, Saint Peter's — Easter: the king climbs the steps on his knees
stops.campa: Leaving the siege at Pavia, Charles rides south and on Holy Saturday sees Rome for the first time in his life. Pope Hadrian, taken by surprise, sends the banners of the city thirty miles up the road; the militia and the schools of the foreigners meet him with palms and crosses, singing. At the steps of Saint Peter's the king of the Franks dismounts and goes up on his knees, kissing each stair one by one, until at the top Hadrian waits and the two men embrace. Easter falls the next day. Within the week Charles renews on the apostle's body his father's donation to Peter.
stops.quote: He kissed every single step one by one as he climbed up to the pontiff.
stops.quote_source: Liber Pontificalis, Life of Hadrian I
suggested_refs: Old Saint Peter's basilica and its atrium steps
the Donation of 774 laid on the tomb of Peter

stops.name: Pavia falls — the Iron Crown of the Lombards
stops.campa: In June, after nine months, plague and famine open the gates of Pavia. Desiderius is taken with his treasure and sent north to a monastery, to end as a monk the line of Alboin. Charles does what no Frank has done: he does not annex, he assumes — from this day he signs himself king of the Franks AND of the Lombards. The tradition sets on his head the Iron Crown, the golden circlet closed with a slim band of iron beaten from a nail of the True Cross, so that whoever wears Lombardy wears the Passion itself. One king now, both sides of the Alps.
suggested_refs: the Iron Crown in the Cathedral of Monza
San Michele Maggiore, Pavia

segments.name: Spain and the Pass of Roncevaux (777-778)

stops.name: Paderborn — the Saracens of Zaragoza kneel at the Saxon assembly
stops.campa: Charles holds the great assembly for the first time inside Saxony, at Paderborn by the two hundred springs of the Pader, as if the conquest were finished. And into this camp of baptisms rides the unforeseen: Sulayman al-Arabi, governor of Barcelona, with envoys of Zaragoza, offering their cities to the king of the Franks against the emir of Cordoba. The map of the world tilts. Charles, fresh from felling one paganism, hears Spain offered like fruit. Only Widukind is absent from the oath-taking, fled to the Danes — the one empty place at the feast, and the costly one.
suggested_refs: the Pader springs and Carolingian palace, Paderborn

stops.name: Chasseneuil — the queen left behind; Louis born
stops.campa: The host masses for Spain, and at the villa of Chasseneuil in Aquitaine the king leaves Hildegard, great with child. While he is beyond the Pyrenees she is delivered of twin boys; one dies, and the one who lives is named Louis — Hlodowig, Clovis's own name reborn in the family that replaced his line. The canon likes the arithmetic: as Roland dies in the pass, the future emperor is in his cradle. Louis the Pious, who will inherit everything, is born into the very summer of the great defeat.
suggested_refs: royal villa of Chasseneuil-du-Poitou

stops.name: Pamplona — the gates opened
stops.campa: Charles crosses the western passes with half the host — the other half swings through Septimania toward the Ebro — and Pamplona, city of the Basques under Saracen lordship, opens its gates to him. It is smooth, too smooth; the mountain people watch the Frankish column from the ridgelines and say nothing. The two armies are to meet at Zaragoza, where Sulayman's promise waits to be kept. The king rides through Navarre in early summer, the first Christian king in the peninsula since the Goths fell, sure that God is leading him as He led at Pavia.
suggested_refs: old city walls of Pamplona

stops.name: Zaragoza — the promised city refuses
stops.campa: Before the walls of Zaragoza the promise dies. Husayn, master of the city, shuts the gates: he made no oath, and the white walls above the Ebro stay silent against the whole Frankish host. There will be no second Pavia; a siege here, a thousand miles from the Rhine, with Saxony smoking behind him, is impossible, and Charles knows it. He takes hostages and gold, takes Sulayman himself in chains for a broken bargain, and turns the army around. In the Chanson this is where Ganelon's embassy plants treason; in the annals it is simply the turning — the first great enterprise that fails.
suggested_refs: walls of Zaragoza above the Ebro
the Aljaferia's Roman-walled predecessor
sources: Chanson de Roland, laisses 1-52 (the embassy and the treason)

stops.name: Pamplona — the walls razed on the way home
stops.campa: Marching home, Charles stops at Pamplona and throws down its walls to the ground, that it may never rebel — a punishment laid on a city that had opened to him, and the Basques of the mountains watch this too. The revised annals say it plainly: Pampelona destructa. The army turns north into the defiles with its hostages, its wagons of Spanish gold, and, riding with the rear-guard, the prefect of the Breton march, Hruodland, whom the singers will make the nephew of the king. The mountains close over the road like water.
suggested_refs: Pamplona, the razed circuit of 778

stops.name: The Pass of Ibaneta, Roncevaux — the rear-guard set
stops.campa: The fifteenth of August. The host files over the pass of Cize in a column stretched thin by the narrow ground, thick woods on either hand. The baggage and the rear-guard come last, and the canon sets the flower of the palace there: Eggihard master of the table, Anselm count of the palace, Roland of the Breton march — in the Chanson, the Twelve Peers with him and Ganelon's treason already sold to King Marsile. On the heights above Ibaneta the Basques lie in the timber, light-armed, patient, native to the dark of the woods. The main army passes down into Gascony, out of earshot. The trap holds its breath.
stops.quote: Eggihard, the King's steward; Anselm, Count Palatine; and Roland, Governor of the March of Brittany, with very many others, fell in this engagement.
suggested_refs: chapel and pass of Ibaneta
monument to Roland at the pass
sources: epitaph of Eggihard (dating the battle to 15 August)

stops.name: Roncevaux — Roland refuses the horn
stops.campa: The heathen host pours down the slopes — a hundred thousand in the song — and Oliver climbs a pine and sees the valley bright with hauberks. Three times he begs Roland: sound the oliphant, Charles will hear and turn the army. Three times Roland refuses. He will not shame his kin, will not have sweet France lowered for his sake. Oliver is wise, says the song, and Roland is brave, and the refusal is both the sin and the glory of France. The rear-guard draws Durendal and turns to face the whole of Spain.
stops.quote: Respunt Rollant: 'Jo fereie que fols! / En dulce France en perdreie mun los.'
suggested_refs: Roland refusing the horn (medieval illuminations)
'Rollant est proz e Oliver est sage'

stops.name: Roncevaux — the Oliphant blown at last
stops.campa: The Peers are falling; sixty men stand of twenty thousand. Now Roland says he will sound the horn, and it is Oliver who refuses him in bitter grief — too late, the blood is spilt. Archbishop Turpin parts them: the horn cannot save them, but Charles will come to avenge and bury them. Then Roland sets the oliphant to his mouth and blows with such force that the veins of his temples burst; the bright blood springs from his mouth. Thirty leagues away the sound reaches Charles: 'Our men give battle,' says the king. Ganelon answers that it is nothing. The mountains carry the horn three times.
stops.quote: Rollant ad mis l'olifan a sa buche, / Empeint le ben, par grant vertut le sunet... / Par mi la buche en salt fors li cler sancs, / De sun cervel le temple en est rumpant.
suggested_refs: the so-called Oliphant of Roland (ivory horns of the treasuries)
Roland sounding the horn, Chartres window

stops.name: Roncevaux — Durendal against the stone
stops.campa: Roland, dying, feels his sight go and thinks of the sword. Durendal must not fall to the pagans — in its golden hilt are sealed a tooth of Saint Peter, blood of Saint Basil, hair of Saint Denis, a piece of the raiment of the Virgin. Ten times he strikes the dark stone; the steel grates and will not break, will not even notch, and springs back toward heaven. He laments over it as over a bride: the conquests they made together, the emperor's beard, sweet France. Unable to break it he lays himself upon it, sword and oliphant beneath his body, so that even his corpse guards them.
stops.quote: E! Durendal, cum es bele e clere e blanche! / Cuntre soleill si luises e reflambes!
suggested_refs: the blade of Rocamadour called Durendal
the cleft rock, Breche de Roland, in the high Pyrenees

stops.name: Roncevaux — Roland dies facing Spain
stops.campa: He goes at a run — dying, he still runs — up under a pine on a little hill, and lies down on the green grass face toward Spain, sword and horn beneath him, so that Charles and all his host shall say he died a conqueror, his face to the enemy. He confesses his sins, beats his breast, and holds up his right glove to God as a vassal returns his fief. Saint Gabriel and Saint Michael of the Peril come down with cherubim and carry the count's soul into Paradise. On the field around him twenty thousand Franks lie dead, and not one with his wounds behind.
stops.quote: Desuz un pin i est alet curant, / Sur l'erbe verte s'i est culchet adenz, / Desuz lui met s'espee e l'olifan, / Turnat sa teste vers la paiene gent.
suggested_refs: the death of Roland (Grandes Chroniques miniatures)
the proffered glove: 'Seint Gabriel de sa main l'ad pris'

stops.name: Roncevaux — the emperor turns back too late
stops.campa: Charles comes back through the pass with the host at the gallop, and for him God works the great wonder: the sun stands still in heaven, halted so the Franks may hunt the pagans into the Ebro before dark. But at Roncevaux there is nothing left to save. The emperor rides among the dead calling for his nephew, for the archbishop, for Oliver, and no one answers; he finds Roland under the pine and faints upon the body, tearing his white beard. A hundred thousand Franks weep with him. The annals say drily that the baggage was lost and the enemy scattered beyond vengeance.
stops.quote: Carles escriet: 'U estes vos, bels nies? / U est l'arcevesque? E li quens Oliver?'
suggested_refs: Chapel of Sancti Spiritus (Silo of Charlemagne), Roncesvalles
the halted sun over the Ebro

stops.name: Blaye — the three biers in Saint-Romain
stops.campa: The emperor has the hearts of Roland, Oliver and Turpin wrapped in silk and their bodies borne down through Gascony; the Gironde is crossed in great ships, and at Blaye, in the basilica of Saint-Romain, the three lords are laid in white sarcophagi. There the song leaves them: la gisent li baron — there lie the barons. For a thousand years pilgrims on the Compostela road will turn aside at Blaye to stand over Roland, and at Bordeaux, on the altar of Saint-Seurin, the oliphant itself is laid up, filled with gold. Charles rides north to learn the Saxons have risen the moment his back was turned.
stops.quote: En blancs sarcous fait metre les seignurs / A Seint Romain: la gisent li baron.
suggested_refs: ruined basilica of Saint-Romain, Blaye
the oliphant on the altar of Saint-Seurin, Bordeaux
sources: Pilgrim's Guide of the Codex Calixtinus (the tombs at Blaye)

stops.name: The Suntel hills — the host cut down among the trees
stops.campa: Widukind is back from the Danes and Saxony burns again. A Frankish force under the king's chamberlain, marshal and counts, jealous of sharing glory, charges up into the Suntel hills without order, each man riding as fast as his horse can carry him, as if racing rather than attacking. In the trees the Saxons close around them. Two of the king's officers, four counts and twenty noblemen die with the men who followed them — the worst Frankish blood spilled in the whole thirty years' war. The news comes to Charles and something in the king goes cold and exact.
suggested_refs: the Suntel ridge above the Weser

stops.name: Verden on the Aller — the terrible number
stops.campa: Charles comes into Saxony with the anger of a king and a bereaved lord, and at Verden, where the Aller meets the Weser, the Saxon nobles deliver up the men of the rebellion — all but Widukind, who is gone again over the Elbe. The canon writes the number without flinching, and this register keeps it as written: four thousand five hundred Saxons, handed over, and beheaded in one day by the river. Then the king goes to winter quarters. The Aller runs to the sea. The chronicle passes to the next year's business, and the reader hears in the silence the sound the axes made from morning until dark.
stops.quote: He had as many as four thousand five hundred of them, who had been handed over, beheaded in one day at the place called Verden on the river Aller.
suggested_refs: the Sachsenhain grove of stones at Verden
Verden cathedral by the Aller

stops.name: The Eresburg — the king winters inside Saxony
stops.campa: For the first time Charles does not go home when the season turns: he keeps Christmas and then Easter at the Eresburg, wife and children with him, holding the winter itself as a conquered province. From the rock where the Irminsul's treasure was carried off, he sends columns out along the frozen rivers, burning the war out of the land month by month. It is the strategy of a man who has understood that Saxony cannot be defeated in summers; it must be inhabited. In the spring the assembly meets at Paderborn, and the roads of Saxony lie open in every direction.
suggested_refs: Obermarsberg winter camp of 784-785

stops.name: Attigny — Widukind baptized, the emperor his godfather
stops.campa: Worn down at last, Widukind asks for pledges, and the king sends them; and the man who burned the churches of the border for thirteen years crosses into Francia and comes to the royal villa of Attigny. There he is baptized, and Charles himself lifts his great enemy from the font, receiving him as a godson and honoring him with magnificent gifts. The war-leader of the old gods goes down into the water and comes up a Frank in white. The annals report that Saxony was then wholly subdued, and the register lets the sentence stand with its whole cost inside it — the pillar, the Aller, the font.
stops.quote: Then Widukind and Abbio came with their companions to Attigny, and there they were baptized, and the lord king raised Widukind from the font.
suggested_refs: royal villa of Attigny
the baptismal gifts of Widukind (later legend of the white horse banner)

stops.name: Ingelheim — Tassilo shorn
stops.campa: At the palace of Ingelheim the assembly sits in judgment on Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, cousin of the king, last of the Agilolfings. The charge is old and cold: harisliz, desertion of the host of Pepin thirty years before, warmed over with his Lombard wife's intrigues and dealings with the Avars. His own men accuse him. The Franks condemn him to death, and Charles, merciful as a door closing, commutes it: the duke is tonsured and sent into a monastery, his sons likewise, his duchy dissolved into the realm. Bavaria is folded in without a battle. The last of the old ducal houses ends under the scissors.
suggested_refs: Kaiserpfalz of Ingelheim
Tassilo Chalice at Kremsmuenster

stops.name: Regensburg — the Avar war launched
stops.campa: From Regensburg on the Danube the king moves against the Avars, the horse-lords of Pannonia who have sat two centuries on the plunder of the Balkans behind their rings of earthwork. Before the host crosses the Enns, three days of litanies, fasting and masses are decreed — the whole army praying itself clean for a holy war. Then the columns move down both banks of the Danube with a fleet between them. The Avar khagans abandon their forward walls without a fight; the Franks march to the Raab through a country that empties before them like a tide going out.
suggested_refs: Porta Praetoria and Carolingian Regensburg
the three-day litanies of 791

stops.name: The Fossa Carolina — the canal between the seas
stops.campa: The king conceives a work no Caesar finished: to join the Rhine to the Danube — the Ocean to the Black Sea — by a canal between the Rezat and the Altmuehl, so that fleets may pass from the North Sea to the Avar war. Thousands of men dig through the autumn; the king comes in person and stays on the works. But rain without end turns the spoil to porridge, the marshy ground gives back by night what is dug by day, and the great trench is abandoned — a scar of water in the Franconian fields, dreaming of ships.
suggested_refs: the Karlsgraben at Graben bei Treuchtlingen

stops.name: Frankfurt — the great synod; Tassilo's last renunciation
stops.campa: In the king's hall at Frankfurt a council of the whole West sits under Charles as under a new Constantine: the adoptionist heresy of Spain is condemned, the Greek council on images is rebuked, weights, measures and the price of bread are fixed as if doctrine and grain were one governance — and they are. Tassilo is led from his cloister one last time to renounce Bavaria forever for himself and his children, and is led back to the silence. In this same summer Queen Fastrada dies. The synod scatters carrying capitularies to every corner of the realm: the empire exists in all but name.
suggested_refs: Council of Frankfurt 794
Libri Carolini
sources: capitulary of the Synod of Frankfurt

stops.name: The Ring of the Avars — the hoard of two centuries
stops.campa: The khaganate, gnawed hollow by its own civil wars, falls open. Eric of Friuli's riders and then Pippin the king's son break into the Ring itself — the ninefold earthwork palace between Danube and Tisza where the tribute of Byzantium and the loot of two hundred years lie heaped in the dark. The treasure is loaded onto fifteen great wagons, each drawn by four oxen, and creaks west across Europe to Aachen. Einhard says plainly: in living memory no war ever made the Franks so rich. The Avars, who were a terror for two centuries, cease so utterly that their own proverb survives them: they perished like the Avars.
stops.quote: All the money and treasure that had been years amassing was seized, and no war in which the Franks have ever engaged within the memory of man brought them such riches and such booty.
suggested_refs: the fifteen ox-wagons of the Avar hoard
gold of the Avar treasure (Vrap and Nagyszentmiklos finds as its shadow)

stops.name: Aachen — the hoard arrives; the gold that pays for everything
stops.campa: The wagons come up the last road to Aachen and the treasure of the steppe is poured out before the king. He gives with both hands: a great share to Rome for Peter, swords and gold to Offa of Mercia, gifts to every church and every faithful man, alms sent even to the Christians of Africa and Syria. The Avar gold gilds the chapel rising over the hot springs, pays the copyists, the marble-haulers, the bronze-founders. The plunder of the pagan Ring becomes the endowment of the Christian empire — the canon's own economy of grace, minted and spent.
suggested_refs: letters of Alcuin on the Avar treasure
gifts to Offa of Mercia

segments.name: Aachen, New Rome, and the Crown of the World (794-800)

stops.name: Aachen — the capital chosen on the hot springs
stops.campa: The king, who has spent his life in the saddle between villas, chooses at last a fixed seat: Aachen, where hot water rises out of the earth as it did for the Romans, whose broken bath-stones still litter the ground. He loves the springs with his whole enormous body — swims a hundred men at a time into the great bath, courtiers, sons, guards, and none can outswim him. Here the palace rises: hall, gallery, treasury, and the chapel to come. The wandering kingship of the Franks puts down a root into warm water, and the root becomes a capital.
stops.quote: He enjoyed the exhalations from natural warm springs, and often practised swimming, in which he was such an adept that none could surpass him.
suggested_refs: the hot springs of Aachen
site of the Carolingian palace under the Rathaus

stops.name: Aachen — Alcuin and the palace school; the tablets under the pillow
stops.campa: Alcuin of York, master of the palace school, has gathered the learned of every nation — Peter of Pisa, Paul the Deacon, Theodulf the Goth — and the court becomes an academy where the king sits as a pupil, nicknamed David among his Homers and Flaccuses. Charles speaks Latin like his own tongue and understands Greek. And at night the emperor of the Franks keeps wax tablets under his pillow, and in wakeful hours brings his great sword-hand to the forming of letters — begun too late, Einhard says tenderly, and meeting with ill success. The copyists multiply; the minuscule spreads; antiquity is recopied into survival.
stops.quote: He also tried to write, and used to keep tablets and blanks in bed under his pillow, that at leisure hours he might accustom his hand to form the letters; however, as he did not begin his efforts in due season, but late in life, they met with ill success.
suggested_refs: Carolingian minuscule
Godescalc Evangelistary
Alcuin's letters to 'David'

stops.name: Ravenna — the marbles of the Caesars taken down
stops.campa: With the pope's written leave, the king's men move through Ravenna, city of the last Western emperors, and take down what the chapel needs: columns of porphyry and green marble, cut for Theodoric and for Justinian's exarchs, lowered from the old palaces onto ox-carts and river barges for the long haul over the Alps. Mosaics are studied, measures taken of San Vitale's octagon — the very geometry of empire packed for export. Rome and Ravenna are quarried not as ruins but as ancestors: the stones are made to migrate north, so that the new Rome may stand on the bones of the old.
suggested_refs: San Vitale, Ravenna
the porphyry and marble columns now in the Aachen octagon
sources: letter of Pope Hadrian granting the marbles

stops.name: Aachen — the Palatine Chapel rising: the octagon, the bronze, the throne
stops.campa: Odo of Metz raises the octagon: eight mighty piers, the sixteen-sided cloak around them, the dome closing overhead like a crown seen from inside. The doors are cast whole in bronze with lions' heads — founding on a scale unseen since Rome fell — and the Ravenna columns go up into the arches. In the western gallery, facing the altar of the Savior, stands the throne: six plain slabs of pale marble, steps worn already as if by centuries that have not yet happened. No gold on it. Whoever sits there sits above the people and below Christ in His dome, which is the whole theory of the empire, built.
stops.quote: He built the beautiful basilica at Aix-la-Chapelle, which he adorned with gold and silver and lamps, and with rails and doors of solid brass. He had the columns and marbles for this structure brought from Rome and Ravenna.
suggested_refs: the Palatine Chapel octagon
the Wolfstuer bronze doors
the marble throne of Charlemagne

stops.name: Paderborn — the blinded pope comes seeing
stops.campa: In Rome, in the April procession, the kinsmen of the old pope fall on Leo III, throw him down, and set upon his eyes and tongue with knives, then leave him in a cell. And God gives back what was cut: the pope's sight and speech are restored whole. Leo escapes down the wall by night and is carried across the Alps to Charles at Paderborn, where the king of the Franks receives the wounded papacy into a Saxon camp. All that winter Alcuin writes to his David: on you alone the churches of Christ now lean. The road to the crown opens from this camp.
stops.quote: On you alone the whole salvation of the churches of Christ rests.
suggested_refs: Karlsburg at Paderborn (meeting of king and pope)
the epic 'Karolus Magnus et Leo Papa'
sources: Liber Pontificalis, Life of Leo III

stops.name: Mentana (Nomentum) — the pope waits twelve miles from Rome
stops.campa: Charles comes south at last to judge the accusations against the vicar of Peter — an unheard-of thing, a Frank sitting over the pope's honor — and Leo III comes out to meet him at Nomentum, the twelfth milestone, an honor given by popes to the emperors of old. They dine together; the pope returns ahead to prepare the city. The next day Rome receives Charles with the banners of the militia and the acclamations of the schools on the steps of Saint Peter's. Everyone in the city knows something is being prepared; the canon lets the king alone not know it.
suggested_refs: the twelfth milestone of the Via Nomentana
sources: Liber Pontificalis, Life of Leo III

stops.name: Saint Peter's — the oath of purgation
stops.campa: In the basilica, before the synod of Franks and Romans that has weighed the charges and found no man willing to judge the apostolic see, Leo III mounts the ambo of his own will, lays his hand on the Gospels, and swears before God and Saint Peter that he is innocent of the crimes charged against him. The assembly sings the Te Deum. On the same day, as if heaven were clearing the whole ledger at once, a priest from Jerusalem delivers to Charles the keys of the Holy Sepulchre and of Calvary, with a banner of the holy city. Two days remain until Christmas.
suggested_refs: the purgation oath of Leo III
the keys of the Holy Sepulchre
sources: Liber Pontificalis, Life of Leo III

stops.name: Saint Peter's, Rome — Christmas Day: the imperial coronation
stops.campa: Mass of the Nativity in Old Saint Peter's. The king of the Franks kneels long in prayer before the confession of the apostle. As he rises, Leo III sets a crown upon his head — and the Roman people, as if one throat, cry out three times the acclamation, and the age turns: to Charles Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-giving emperor of the Romans, life and victory. The pope anoints him and then does reverence before him. Three hundred and twenty-four years after the last emperor of the West was unmade, there is an emperor in Rome again, and he is a Frank.
stops.quote: Karolo, piissimo Augusto, a Deo coronato, magno et pacifico imperatori, vita et victoria!
stops.quote_source: Liber Pontificalis, Life of Leo III (the triple acclamation); cf. Royal Frankish Annals 801
suggested_refs: the coronation of Charlemagne (Raphael workshop fresco, Vatican)
mosaic of the Lateran triclinium: Peter giving Leo the pallium and Charles the banner
sources: Liber Pontificalis, Life of Leo III

stops.name: Saint Peter's — the emperor's protest, recorded forever
stops.campa: The canon keeps, beside the acclamation, the emperor's own recoil, set down by the man who knew him best. Charles declared afterward that had he known the pope's design he would not have entered the church that day, though it was the greatest feast of the year. The register holds both truths at once, as the tradition does: the crown desired and the crown ambushed, God's plan and the pope's timing, the emperor made before he consents. He wears it, protesting, for the rest of his life — and never again lets a pope hold the crown first.
stops.quote: He at first had such an aversion that he declared that he would not have set foot in the Church the day that they were conferred, although it was a great feast-day, if he could have foreseen the design of the Pope.
suggested_refs: Einhard's Vita Karoli, chapter 28

stops.name: Portovenere — Abul-Abbas the elephant lands in Italy
stops.campa: Isaac the Jew, sent four years before as the emperor's envoy to Harun al-Rashid, king of the Persians, returns out of Africa with the caliph's gift walking behind him: an elephant. The beast has come from Baghdad to the coast, over the sea in a ship built or found to bear him, and in October he steps ashore at Portovenere on the Ligurian rock. Italy has not seen his kind since the triumphs of Rome. Children run from the harbor to touch and flee; the mountains stand between the elephant and his emperor, and the snow is already on the passes.
suggested_refs: harbor of Portovenere
Harun al-Rashid's embassy gifts

stops.name: Vercelli — the elephant winters below the Alps
stops.campa: The Alps cannot be crossed; the snow lies deep on the Mont Cenis where armies passed in autumn, and an elephant is not an army. So Isaac and Abul-Abbas turn into winter quarters at Vercelli in the rice-flat plain of the Po, and a Lombard town spends a winter feeding, stabling and marveling at a beast out of the book of Maccabees. Hay is requisitioned; a barn is a palace. In the spring, says the annalist with perfect calm, they will walk over the mountains. The elephant waits out the snow like a patient ambassador, which is what he is.
stops.quote: Because he could not cross the Alps on account of the snow, he wintered at Vercelli.
suggested_refs: Vercelli in the Po plain

stops.name: Aachen — the missi ride out; the empire ordered
stops.campa: In this year the emperor reorganizes the realm as a man reorders his house: the great capitulary goes out, and pairs of missi dominici — one count, one bishop, the emperor's eyes doubled — ride circuits into every province to hear the widow and the orphan, to correct the judges, to take from every free man above twelve a new oath to Charles as emperor. Law is written down for Saxon and Frisian and Lombard alike; the survey-takers count and record. The empire becomes a thing of parchment as much as of swords — riders on all roads, carrying the emperor's justice in saddlebags.
stops.quote: The most serene and most Christian lord emperor Charles has chosen from his nobles the wisest and most prudent men... and sent them through his whole kingdom.
suggested_refs: Capitulare missorum generale of 802
the missi dominici

stops.name: Aachen — the elephant delivered to the emperor
stops.campa: On the twentieth of July Isaac comes up the road to Aachen with the elephant and all the gifts of the king of the Persians, and delivers everything to the emperor in his palace. The annalist gives the beast a full sentence and his name: the elephant's name was Abul Abaz. The gray mountain kneels in the palace yard; the court of the Franks stands in a ring, utterly silenced. Baghdad has bowed to Aachen in the most magnificent way one empire can bow to another — by sending it a living wonder. He will live at the emperor's side eight years.
stops.quote: The name of the elephant was Abul Abaz.
suggested_refs: Abul-Abbas in the palace yard at Aachen
the water-clock and gifts of Harun al-Rashid

stops.name: Thionville — the ordering of the succession
stops.campa: At the winter palace of Thionville on the Moselle the emperor gathers the magnates and divides the future: the Divisio Regnorum, sealed the sixth of February, parts the empire among the three sons of Hildegard — Charles the eldest to Francia, Pippin to Italy, Louis to Aquitaine — with careful clauses for peace between brothers and none at all for the imperial title, which the emperor keeps folded in God's hand. Copies go to Rome for the pope's subscription. It is prudent, paternal, complete — and heaven will annul it clause by clause, taking the sons before the father.
suggested_refs: Divisio Regnorum of 806

stops.name: Aachen — the water-clock of brass strikes the hours
stops.campa: New envoys of Harun al-Rashid reach the court bearing, among silks, perfumes and a pavilion-tent of marvelous size, a clock of brass driven by water: at each hour the number of bronze balls falls ringing on a cymbal beneath, and twelve horsemen ride out of twelve doors, shutting behind them the windows that stood open. The Franks crowd the machine to watch time itself perform. It is the East's second great sermon to the West — first a beast, now an engine — and the annalist describes its workings with the wonder of a man describing an angel's anatomy.
stops.quote: A clock of brass, a marvelous mechanical contraption, in which the course of the twelve hours moved according to a water clock... and twelve horsemen who at the end of each hour stepped out of twelve windows, closing the previously open windows by their movements.
suggested_refs: the water-clock of Harun al-Rashid
the caliph's pavilion at Aachen

stops.name: Milan — Pippin the son dies
stops.campa: Pippin, king of Italy, the emperor's second son — the boy who broke into the Avar Ring, the king who warred on Venice in her lagoons — dies of sickness in Italy on the eighth of July, thirty-three years old, and is buried at Milan in Sant'Ambrogio. The Divisio of Thionville loses its southern third; a bastard grandson, Bernard, will be set over Italy in his place. The emperor is on the Danish war when the news rides north. The canon begins here the drumbeat of the griefs: heaven is emptying the emperor's table one seat at a time.
suggested_refs: Sant'Ambrogio, Milan (tomb of King Pippin of Italy)

stops.name: Lippeham on the Rhine — the death of Abul-Abbas
stops.campa: Godofrid king of the Danes has harried Frisia with two hundred ships, and the emperor, past sixty, calls out the host and takes the elephant on campaign — the living standard of the empire marching against the north. At Lippeham, where the Lippe meets the Rhine, the army waits on the muster; and there Abul-Abbas, nine years a Frank, dies suddenly. The annalist gives him a death-notice among kings and battles, without apology. The emperor has lost, in one summer, a son and an elephant, and the canon records both griefs in the same annal-year, side by side.
stops.quote: There the elephant which Aaron, the king of the Saracens, had sent him, died a sudden death.
suggested_refs: confluence of Lippe and Rhine near Wesel
later legend of the elephant's bones

stops.name: The camp on the Danish march — the fireball throws the emperor from his horse
stops.campa: On this same last Saxon campaign, riding out of camp before daybreak, the emperor sees a ball of fire fall suddenly across the clear sky, blazing from right to left through the darkness. As all men stare, his horse drops headlong and throws him so hard against the ground that the clasp of his cloak snaps and his sword-belt is torn from him; the attendants who run to him must unarm the emperor of the West where he lies in the dirt. The javelin in his fist is flung twenty feet clear. The register does not soften it: heaven has begun addressing him directly.
stops.quote: Charles himself saw a ball of fire fall suddenly from the heavens with a great light, just as he was leaving camp before sunrise to set out on the march... the horse which he was riding gave a sudden plunge, head foremost, and fell, and threw him to the ground so heavily that his cloak buckle was broken and his sword belt shattered.
suggested_refs: Einhard's catalogue of omens, Vita Karoli 32

stops.name: Aachen — the death of Charles the Younger; the emperor weeps
stops.campa: On the fourth of December dies Charles the Younger, the eldest, the soldier-son shaped in his father's image, heir of Francia and of the great name — unmarried, childless, suddenly, of a stroke. Of the three kings among whom Thionville parted the world, only Louis of Aquitaine is left alive. Einhard, who watched, wrote that the emperor bore the deaths of his sons and of his daughter Rotrud with less patience than his greatness of soul had promised: his affection mastered him, and he wept. The strongest man of the age sits in the octagon's gallery and cries like any father, and the canon honors him for it.
stops.quote: When his sons and his daughter died, he was not so calm as might have been expected from his remarkably strong mind, for his affections were no less strong, and moved him to tears.
suggested_refs: the emptied Divisio of 806

segments.name: The Omens and the Throne in the Tomb (813-1215)

stops.name: Mainz — the bridge of ten years burns in three hours
stops.campa: The wooden bridge at Mainz — five hundred paces over the Rhine, ten years in the building, the emperor's proudest work of peace, which he meant one day to remake in stone — catches fire and is so utterly consumed in three hours that not one splinter remains above the waterline. The river carries off the charcoal of a decade. Einhard sets it first among the portents of the end: the works of the reign have begun to be recalled, as a lord recalls his loans. The emperor, they say, receives the news in silence.
stops.quote: The wooden bridge over the Rhine at Mayence... was so completely consumed in three hours by an accidental fire that not a single splinter of it was left, except what was under water.
suggested_refs: site of the Carolingian Rhine bridge at Mainz

stops.name: Aachen — the portico falls; the word PRINCEPS fades from the wall
stops.campa: The omens gather at Aachen itself. On Ascension Day the gallery between basilica and palace, built with such pains, falls suddenly in ruins to the ground. The sun and moon are repeatedly darkened; a black spot sits on the sun for seven days. Lightning strikes the chapel and the gilded apple falls from the roof-ridge. And in the red-painted inscription that rings the dome, between BASILICA and the name of God, the word PRINCEPS — Karolus Princeps — fades letter by letter until, months before the end, it cannot be read at all. He says he takes no account of such things. He orders nothing repainted.
stops.quote: The letters of the word Princeps were so effaced as to be no longer decipherable... But Charles despised, or affected to despise, all these omens, as having no reference whatever to him.
suggested_refs: the dome inscription of the Palatine Chapel
Einhard's omen catalogue

stops.name: Aachen, the Palatine Chapel — with his own hands he crowns Louis
stops.campa: The emperor summons Louis from Aquitaine, and on the eleventh of September, in the octagon, wearing his crown, he leads his last son to the altar where a second crown lies. No pope is present; none has been invited. He asks the people if it pleases them — they cry that it is God's will — and the emperor with his own hands sets the crown on Louis and names him consort of the imperial name. The lesson of Christmas 800 is delivered back to history: the empire of the Franks crowns itself. The octagon holds them both under its dome like two figures in one reliquary.
stops.quote: He placed a crown upon his head and made him partner in the imperial name.
suggested_refs: the throne gallery of the Palatine Chapel
Thegan's account of the self-crowning of 813

stops.name: Aachen — the last winter: fever, the seventh day
stops.campa: In January, after the autumn's hunting, a high fever takes him in the bath-warm palace, and he doctors himself as he always has, by fasting, believing illness can be starved like a besieged town. Pleurisy settles into the side of the swimmer of Aachen. He keeps to his bed and takes almost nothing but a little water. The court moves on tiptoe through halls built for his stride. On the seventh day he asks for his chaplain and receives the holy communion; those at the bedside see him gathering himself, deliberately, as for one more crossing of the Alps.
suggested_refs: the palace precinct of Aachen

stops.name: Aachen — the death of the emperor
stops.campa: On the twenty-eighth of January, at nine in the morning, having received the sacrament, Charles dies in the seventy-second year of his life and the forty-seventh of his reign. He signs himself, they say, with the cross, composes his own limbs on the bed, and sings under his breath the verse: into thy hands I commend my spirit. The news goes out from Aachen like a change of weather over the whole of the West; Louis comes from Aquitaine to an empire already draped. Einhard, who loved him, writes the date with a clerk's plainness and lets the plainness carry the grief.
stops.quote: He died January twenty-eighth, the seventh day from the time that he took to his bed, at nine o'clock in the morning, after partaking of the holy communion, in the seventy-second year of his age and the forty-seventh of his reign.
suggested_refs: the obit of 28 January in the martyrologies

stops.name: The Palatine Chapel — the entombment and the golden epitaph
stops.campa: He had named no burial place; all agree none could be more fitting than the basilica he built. He is buried the same day he died — washed, cared for, carried into the octagon amid the greatest lamentation of the whole people, and laid beneath a gilded arch with his image above, and the inscription set in gold letters: here lies the body of Charles, the great and orthodox emperor, who nobly enlarged the kingdom of the Franks and reigned prosperously forty-seven years. The dome he raised closes over him. The word MAGNUS enters the grave with him and never leaves the language again.
stops.quote: Sub hoc conditorio situm est corpus Karoli, Magni atque Orthodoxi Imperatoris, qui regnum Francorum nobiliter ampliavit et per annos XLVII feliciter rexit.
suggested_refs: the Proserpina sarcophagus of Aachen
the lost gilded arcus over the tomb

stops.name: The vault beneath the octagon — the emperor seated in the tomb
stops.campa: And this is what the register keeps beneath the pavement: the emperor does not lie down. The tradition seats him in the vault on a throne as one living — crowned with gold, sceptred, girt with the sword, the pilgrim's scrip of Compostela at his side, and on his knees the Gospel, open, his gloved finger at the page. The tomb is sealed and filled with treasures and spices, and the seated king begins his long audience in the dark: the emperor who does not die but waits, the sleeping king of the mountain before there was a mountain, holding the Word open at the place where he stopped reading.
suggested_refs: the seated-emperor legend of the Aachen vault
the Sleeping Emperor motif (Kyffhaeuser's ancestor)
sources: Chronicon Novaliciense III.32 (retrospective witness to the tradition)

stops.name: Aachen — Otto III opens the vault in the year 1000
stops.campa: At Pentecost of the millennial year Emperor Otto III has the pavement of the chapel broken and goes down with Count Otto of Lomello into the vault. They find him as the register promised: not lying as the dead lie, but seated on a throne as if alive, the golden crown on the skull, the sceptre in gloved hands — and the fingernails, grown on in death, have pierced through the gloves. Nothing has fallen away but the tip of the nose, which Otto restores in gold. He clothes the dead emperor in white, cuts the nails, takes one tooth for a relic, and seals the tomb.
stops.quote: He was not lying, as the bodies of other dead men lie, but sat upon a throne as though living, crowned with a golden crown, holding a sceptre in gloved hands, through which his fingernails had grown and pierced.
stops.quote_source: Chronicon Novaliciense III.32 (the account of Count Otto of Lomello)
suggested_refs: Otto III enthroned (Gospels of Otto III)
the golden nose-tip of the year 1000

stops.name: Aachen — the canonization of the emperor
stops.campa: On the twenty-ninth of December 1165, at the urging of Frederick Barbarossa, the bones are raised from the vault and Charles is enrolled among the saints of God — Sanctus Karolus — Aachen decked for the elevation, the imperial court attending its own ancestor onto the altars. The emperor of the Franks becomes a saint of the empire he made, his relics parted into arm and skull reliquaries of gold, his cult kept at Aachen. The kingdom he anointed returns the favor: France's kings march under Saint Charlemagne, and Joan of Orleans names him among the saints of the kingdom she will call holy.
suggested_refs: the Bust of Charlemagne (Aachen treasury)
the arm reliquary of Charlemagne

stops.name: Aachen — the last nail: the emperor sealed in the golden shrine
stops.campa: Two days after his own crowning at Aachen, Frederick II comes into the chapel where the bones of the saint-emperor lie in the great golden Karlsschrein, wrought like a church of gold. The new king of the Romans takes hammer and nails and with his own hand drives the last nails home, sealing Charlemagne into the shrine forever. The circle closes: crowned unawares by a pope, he is nailed into gold by an emperor's hand. There he lies to this day under the octagon — the bearded Charles of the Chanson, France's and the empire's dream of the just king, seated, waiting, the Gospel open on his knees.
suggested_refs: the Karlsschrein in Aachen cathedral
the throne of Charlemagne above, still facing the altar
